Quantum tunneling lets positively charged nuclei overcome electrical repulsion and fuse

evaluation_claims.text: Stars shine because of nuclear fusion reactions taking place in their cores.
The most common and fundamental reaction across the universe is the fusion of hydrogen into helium.
The net process of hydrogen fusion converts four free protons into a single helium nucleus.
The energy released from an individual conversion of four protons into helium is exceedingly small, but countless reactions occur every second.
The collective energy release from fusion maintains the high internal temperatures that generate outward gas pressure, which holds up the star's outer layers against gravitational collapse.
A star's lifespan is determined by its mass, its composition, and its nuclear fusion reactions.
The lifetime of a fuel-consuming system equals the total amount of available fuel divided by the consumption rate.
A star's total fuel reservoir for nuclear fusion is proportional to its initial mass.
A more massive star begins life with more hydrogen but is hotter and brighter, consuming its fuel at a much faster rate.
Slight increases in stellar mass produce enormous increases in stellar luminosity.
Massive stars burn through their fuel rapidly and live significantly shorter lives than small stars.
Stars with higher proportions of heavy elements burn through their fuel faster, reducing their lifespan.
A star like the Sun has enough core hydrogen to sustain helium synthesis for roughly ten billion years.
A star of twenty-five solar masses builds up layers of heavy elements and consumes its entire fuel supply in about eight million years.
When core hydrogen is depleted, the predominantly helium core is initially too cool to initiate helium fusion.
The depleted core contracts under gravity, releasing gravitational potential energy and heating up.
The extra heat triggers hydrogen fusion in a shell around the core, causing the outer layers to swell, cool, and expand into a red giant.
As stars evolve, they can fuse progressively heavier elements such as helium, carbon, and oxygen.
Each successive fusion reaction yields less energy than the preceding one, causing the star's energy output to decline over time.
In very massive stars, fusion continues until an inert iron-56 core forms.
Iron cannot release energy through fusion; fusing it requires an energy input, making it stable against further fusion.
When the iron core contracts and temperatures rise, iron nuclei disintegrate into alpha particles, draining energy from the core.
When outward pressure fails, the outer layers collapse inward and the star undergoes a core-collapse supernova.
When a star can no longer generate energy to counteract gravity, it collapses into a final remnant (white dwarf, neutron star, or black hole) depending on its initial mass.
Stars sustain themselves by fusing light nuclei into heavier ones, liberating energy that supports their structure against gravity.

reference_verifications.rationale: Directly stated: stars shine because of nuclear fusion reactions in their core.
Evidence says the most common fusion reaction (in stars) is hydrogen into helium; 'across the universe' and 'fundamental' are broader than stated.
Net reaction converts four free protons to a single helium nucleus.
Energy per net conversion is exceedingly small, so many reactions must occur; large quantities fuse every second.
Many reactions produce enough energy to keep temperature high enough to maintain gas pressure holding up outer layers against gravitational collapse.
Directly stated.
Lifetime = amount of fuel/consumption rate.
Fuel proportional to initial mass when fusion began.
More hydrogen, hotter and brighter, consumption rate far greater.
States slight increases in mass produce large increases in luminosity; 'enormous' slightly stronger but close.
Evidence states massive stars live shorter lives because they consume fuel much faster.
TutorChase states more heavy elements means faster burning and shorter lifespan.
Directly states a Sun-like star has enough hydrogen for helium synthesis for about ten billion years.
Evidence says that within eight million years a 25-solar-mass star builds up layers of heavy elements, but it does not say it consumes its entire fuel supply in that time.
Evidence says the predominantly helium core is too cool to initiate helium fusion once core hydrogen is exhausted.
Evidence says the helium core contracts, releasing gravitational potential energy and growing hotter.
Evidence describes the heating triggering hydrogen shell fusion and outer layers expanding, cooling, and the star becoming a red giant.
Evidence says that as a star runs out of hydrogen it fuses heavier elements such as helium, carbon, and oxygen.
Evidence states each fusion reaction releases less energy than the previous one, so energy output decreases over time.
Evidence says in massive stars an inert iron core forms, and iron-56 cannot fuse without energy input.
Iron-56 fuses only with energy input, so it is stable against further fusion.
Core contracts, reaches temperatures where iron disintegrates into alpha particles, draining energy.
Outer layers collapse onto the core, producing a core-collapse supernova.
Star unable to counteract gravity collapses into a white dwarf, neutron star, or black hole depending on mass.
Fusion of lighter into heavier elements releases energy that sustains the star against gravitational collapse.

citation_entailment_verifications.rationale: Both state stars shine because of nuclear fusion reactions in their core.
Evidence says the most common fusion reaction is hydrogen into helium, but not 'fundamental' nor 'across the universe'.
Net reaction converts four free protons to a single helium nucleus.
Energy per conversion is exceedingly small; many reactions must occur. 'Every second' is a minor extrapolation.
Many reactions produce enough energy to keep temperature high to maintain gas pressure holding up outer layers against gravitational collapse.
Both state the lifespan is determined by mass, composition, and nuclear fusion reactions.
Evidence states lifetime = amount of fuel/consumption rate.
Fuel = k × initial mass, proportional to initial mass.
Massive stars have more hydrogen, consume fuel much faster, and are hotter and brighter.
Evidence says slight mass increases produce large luminosity increases; 'enormous' is stronger wording.
Evidence states massive stars live shorter lives because they consume fuel much faster.
Both state more heavy elements means faster fuel burning and shorter lifespan.
States Sun-like star has enough hydrogen for helium synthesis for about ten billion years.
Supports layers of heavy elements within eight million years, but the evidence doesn't explicitly say entire fuel is consumed in that time (only the snippet 'nuclear fuel' preceding).
States the predominantly helium core is too low a temperature to initiate helium fusion after hydrogen depletion.
Evidence says the core can only contract, releasing gravitational potential energy and growing hotter.
Evidence states the raised temperature allows hydrogen shell fusion, and the outer layers expand and cool into a red giant.
Both passages say that as hydrogen runs out the star fuses heavier elements such as helium, carbon, and oxygen.
Evidence directly states each fusion reaction releases less energy than the previous, so energy output decreases over time.

Evidence describes a 25-solar-mass star forming an inert iron core and iron-56 being stable against fusion. It does not say 'very massive stars' in general, though the example is consistent with the claim.
Evidence says iron-56 fuses only with energy input, so it is stable against further fusion.
Core contracts, reaches temperatures where iron nuclei disintegrate into alpha particles, draining energy.

Evidence says outer layers collapse onto the core resulting in a supernova, but it attributes this to the energy drain/failed support in context; the explicit 'outward pressure fails' wording is implied rather than stated.
Evidence states that when a star can't generate enough energy against gravity it collapses to a white dwarf, neutron star, or black hole depending on mass.
Evidence describes hydrogen fusion into helium releasing energy to hold up outer layers against gravity, but doesn't explicitly generalize to fusing light nuclei into heavier ones.

additional_metric_details.notes: All scores are Claude judgments, not verified ground truth. Repair effectiveness compares coverage/narration, not factual truth. No revision or no retrieval is N/A rather than zero.

metric_semantics.reference_evidence_support_percent: Evidence entailment within the frozen reference corpus; not factual accuracy.
metric_semantics.query_coverage_percent: Coverage of a fixed six-aspect checklist derived once per question from the question text and shared by all systems; missing/duplicate judge outputs are normalized against that fixed denominator.
metric_semantics.narration_input: Coverage, relevance, narration and grounded-requirement judgements use the complete script with [E-...] evidence markers removed; claim extraction and citation metrics use the marked script. Aspect scores are continuous in [0, 1].
metric_semantics.narration_quality_percent: Ten-dimension spoken educational narration score; excludes factual truth.
metric_semantics.citation_precision: Share of emitted citation IDs that are identified as supporting the claim when verification is restricted to cited passages.
metric_semantics.citation_recall: Share of all citation-required extracted factual claims that have at least one cited passage judged to support the claim.
metric_semantics.evaluation_estimated_llm_cost_usd: Evaluator telemetry. CLI mode uses Claude Code's reported list-price equivalent; API mode uses the configured Anthropic per-token rates.
